analysis.one_liner: Shields makers of critical infrastructure equipment from wildfire damage lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would wipe out most lawsuits against manufacturers whose equipment sparks wildfires, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in June 2025 and has had no further action, with 22 Republicans backing it and no Democrat.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies that make critical infrastructure equipment—broadly defined to include electrical grid and other essential hardware—would be immune from lawsuits over wildfires, no matter how careless they were, unless a victim could prove deliberate misconduct in design or production. Someone whose home burned because a manufacturer's equipment ignited a fire could no longer recover in court for negligence. The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers of critical infrastructure equipment, especially electrical equipment and other hardware in the government's 'critical manufacturing' sector. Wildfire liability is a growing, expensive risk—equipment and power lines have ignited deadly fires in several states—so a near-total immunity shield removes a major financial exposure. A handful of the industry's allies in Congress also benefit from a favored issue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Critical infrastructure and electrical equipment manufacturers

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes any manufacturer of critical infrastructure equipment immune from federal and state claims for losses caused by wildfire incidents, unless the victim proves willful misconduct in the design or production of the equipment.

This immunity covers the full range of ordinary lawsuits—negligence, product defects, and other civil claims—so wildfire victims could not recover damages in court for carelessly made equipment that started a fire.

The definitions are broad: 'critical infrastructure' uses the PATRIOT Act definition covering systems and assets vital to the nation, and 'manufacturer' covers the entire critical manufacturing sector, which includes electrical equipment and many other industries.
The bill frames this as supporting the manufacture of secure and resilient critical infrastructure, citing a 2013 presidential policy directive.

analysis.who_pays: People who lose homes, businesses, or family members in wildfires started by manufacturer equipment. They would bear those losses themselves, or shift them to their insurers and to federal disaster aid—meaning taxpayers pick up part of the tab. State and local governments facing fire costs would also lose a way to recover.

drawbacks.text: A homeowner whose house burned because a manufacturer's negligently designed or manufactured equipment ignited a fire would have no remedy in court, because the bill removes liability for everything short of willful misconduct.
The costs of fires caused by company equipment do not disappear; they shift to victims, their insurers, and federal disaster programs funded by taxpayers.
The definitions sweep in the entire critical manufacturing sector under the PATRIOT Act's broad critical-infrastructure language, so the shield would extend far beyond any single industry.
Removing legal consequences for careless manufacturing weakens the ordinary market incentive to make safer equipment, which is the main reason product liability law exists.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Manufacturers gain real, measurable protection from a growing liability risk. But the trade-off is one-sided: the bill takes away the main legal tool fire victims and their communities have to make equipment makers pay for fires their products caused, and it does so with a willful-misconduct standard that is almost impossible to meet in practice. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the bill simply moves wildfire losses from companies to victims and taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 2025 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no vote, and no movement since.

narrative.text: Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks introduced the bill on June 26, 2025, joined by Reps. Bob Latta and Tom Tiffany.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day, the standard first step that sends a bill to the committee with jurisdiction over it.
No further action has been taken—no committee vote, no floor consideration, and no companion Senate action recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one's position has changed. If the bill stays dormant, electrical and other critical-infrastructure equipment makers avoid both new immunity and any accompanying scrutiny of wildfire liability, while fire victims keep the legal rights they have today for the time being.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; no one has moved

for.name: Mariannette Miller-Meeks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

for.name: 21 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Democrat has sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 backers—the sponsor and 21 cosponsors—are Republicans, and no Democrat has joined, but there has been no vote so the full partisan split has not been tested.

industries.industry: Critical infrastructure equipment manufacturers (electrical grid and other critical-manufacturing sectors)
industries.note: The bill gives them near-total immunity from wildfire lawsuits, shifting the cost of fires their equipment causes to victims, insurers, and taxpayers. Their gain is directly the public's loss in court.

Insurers would pay more wildfire claims directly because they could no longer recover from the equipment manufacturer that caused a fire, pushing premiums up; but their own manufacturing-policy customers would face less liability.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat in the House Judiciary Committee for months with no hearing or markup scheduled and no Democratic support. Bills in this position typically die quietly at the end of the Congress unless the committee schedules action, which looks unlikely given the single-party support and the controversy of stripping wildfire victims' legal rights.
